title: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — habitual agreed; actual denied; two entry-modes
pass_a_gloss: We agree habitual sin entered through one man into all—experience confirms it; we do not agree actual entered that way—we deny it flat, and it cannot be proved. Our reading stands as confessed; let opponents prove theirs before it is admitted. Finally the two entry-modes—one feigned, one sure and confessed—are wholly diverse; one beside the other is null or figurative. How can one verb of entering, used once, mean things so unlike?
pass_b_english: Next it is agreed between us that habitual sin entered through one man into all humans, and experience itself confirms it; but it is not agreed that actual sin entered through one man into all humans; for this we flatly deny, and it cannot be proved. Our interpretation therefore cannot be denied, since it is in confession. Those who oppose us must therefore prove their interpretation, before it can or ought to be admitted. Finally since those two modes of entering, of which one is feigned, the other is certain and confessed, are wholly diverse, and one with respect to the other is either nothing or figurative, how can things so diverse be signified by one verb of entering used once?
source_text: Deinde convenit inter nos peccatum habituale per unum hominem in omnes homines intrasse, idque ipsa experientia confirmat; sed non convenit peccatum actuale per unum hominem in omnes homines intrasse; hoc enim pernegamus, neque potest probari. Nostra igitur interpretatio negari non potest, cum sit in confesso. Suam igitur qui nobis adversantur, probent interpretationem necesse est, antequam admitti aut possit aut debeat. Denique cum duo illi introeundi modi, quorum alter fingitur, alter est certus & confessus, prorsus sint diversi, alterque alterius respectu, vel nullus vel figuratus sit, qui potest tam diversa unum introeundi verbum semel usurpatum significare?

choices.choice: Habitual agreed; actual denied; one verb can't mean both
